personalEssay.prompt: Discuss an accomplishment, event, or realization that sparked a period of personal growth and a new understanding of yourself or others.
personalEssay.text:
There is a cardboard box in my closet that has been to six states. It's labeled CALEB: OPEN FIRST, in my mom's handwriting, and it's been taped and re-taped so many times it's more tape than cardboard.

My dad is in the Air Force, which means I've moved five times since kindergarten: from Ohio to Texas, then Georgia, Virginia, Colorado, and now Alaska. Every time, the OPEN FIRST box has the same things in it: a nightlight shaped like a moon (I'm seventeen, I know), a framed photo of my grandparents in Ohio, a Swiss Army knife my grandpa gave me, and a list I started writing when I was eight called "Things That Are the Same Everywhere."

The list began as a kid's coping strategy. I was the new kid again, crying in a strange bedroom in Georgia, and my mom told me to write down everything I knew would be the same at my new school. The first entries are pretty basic. "Recess." "Pizza on Fridays." "The moon." Later ones get more specific. "Some kid will ask if I've been to war." "The library always has a quiet corner." "Somebody will be nice by Wednesday."

For a long time I thought the point of moving was to survive it. Get through the first week, find a lunch table, don't get too attached, because you'll be leaving in two or three years anyway. I got very good at being new. I was so good at it that I never really let myself get past it.

The thing that changed that was Civil Air Patrol. I joined as a freshman in Colorado Springs, mostly because my dad thought I needed something to do besides video games. And I loved it. The uniforms, the aerospace classes, the first time I took the controls of a Cessna on an orientation flight and the instructor let me bank over Pikes Peak. I worked harder than I'd ever worked on anything, and in the fall of my sophomore year I earned the Billy Mitchell Award, which is a big milestone for cadets.

Two months later, we got orders to Alaska.

I remember being angry in a way I hadn't been since I was little. I had finally built something that mattered, and I had to leave it again. But the first week in Anchorage, I looked up the local CAP squadron, and when I walked in, a cadet I'd never met saluted, looked at the Mitchell ribbon on my uniform, and said, "Oh good, you can help teach the new kids." That was it. No awkward first week. No lunch table problem. Just, here's what we need you for.

That moment made me realize something I'd been missing about my own list. "Things That Are the Same Everywhere" wasn't only about what I could expect from a new place. It was also about what I could bring to it. I didn't have to just wait for someone to be nice by Wednesday. I could be the somebody.

Since then, I've tried to live that way. I mentor younger military kids at the youth center on base, especially the ones who just arrived and look the way I used to. I started a snow-shoveling business mostly because I noticed how many families on my street had a parent deployed and nobody to clear the driveway at 6 a.m. Now I'm Cadet Commander of my squadron, and the first thing I do with every new cadet is ask where they moved from.

The OPEN FIRST box is still in my closet. When I leave for college, it will go with me, and I'll open it first like always. But I added a new line to the list this year. "You don't have to wait to belong. You can start."

supplements.prompt: What excites you about the University of Notre Dame that may not be shared by other universities?
supplements.text:
I've lived in six states, so I've learned to notice what makes a place feel like home. At Notre Dame, it seems to be the dorms. I love that students stay in the same residence hall for years, with its own traditions and rivalries and Masses. When you've moved as many times as I have, the idea of a community that keeps you on purpose sounds pretty amazing.

I'm also excited about Notre Dame's Air Force ROTC detachment. Growing up in a military family, I've seen what good leadership looks like and what bad leadership costs people. Civil Air Patrol gave me my first chance to lead, and I want to keep developing that while I study aerospace engineering.

Notre Dame talks about educating the mind and the heart, and I think that matters for anyone who wants to lead other people. I don't just want to learn how to design aircraft. I want to learn how to be the kind of officer, and the kind of person, who notices the new kid in the room.
